notes:
Newton's law of gravitation

  • $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$; $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\,\text{N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}$, a universal constant with the same value everywhere, independent of the medium.

Acceleration due to gravity ($g$)

  • At the surface: $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$.
  • At height $h$: $g' = \dfrac{g}{(1+h/R)^2} \approx g\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{R}\right)$ for $h\ll R$.
  • At depth $d$: $g' = g\left(1-\dfrac{d}{R}\right)$.
  • For the same small distance from the surface, $g$ decreases twice as fast going up as it does going down.

Gravitational potential energy & escape velocity

  • $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ (taken zero at infinity; becomes more negative as $r$ decreases, i.e. as the body is brought closer).
  • Escape velocity $v_e = \sqrt{2gR} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} \approx 11.2\,\text{km s}^{-1}$ for Earth; independent of the mass of the body being projected.

Orbital motion of satellites

  • Orbital velocity close to the surface $v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$; related to escape velocity by $v_e = \sqrt2\,v_o$.
  • Total mechanical energy of an orbiting satellite $= -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ (always negative, hence a bound orbit).
  • Astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft feel weightless because they and the craft are both in continuous free fall with the same acceleration — not because gravity is absent there.
  • Geostationary satellite: time period 24 h, orbits in the equatorial plane in the same sense as Earth's rotation, altitude $\approx 36000$ km.

Kepler's laws

LawStatement
1stOrbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus
2ndEqual areas swept in equal times (a consequence of conservation of angular momentum)
3rd$T^2 \propto r^3$

Exam tip

KCET typically sets 1–2 questions from this chapter, often on the variation of $g$ with height/depth or a Kepler's-third-law ratio problem. Memorise the $v_e=\sqrt2\,v_o$ shortcut — it saves valuable time.

questions.q: Two point masses of 2 kg and 3 kg are placed 1 m apart. The gravitational force of attraction between them ($G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$) is approximately
questions.explanation: $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times2\times3}{1^2} \approx 4\times10^{-10}$ N.

questions.q: If the distance between two point masses is doubled, keeping the masses unchanged, the gravitational force between them becomes
questions.explanation: $F \propto 1/r^2$; doubling $r$ reduces $F$ to $1/2^2 = 1/4$ of its original value.

questions.q: If both masses in a gravitating pair are doubled while the distance between them stays the same, the gravitational force becomes
questions.explanation: $F \propto m_1m_2$; doubling both masses multiplies $F$ by $2\times2 = 4$.

questions.q: At a height equal to the radius of the Earth ($h = R$) above the surface, the acceleration due to gravity is
At a depth equal to half the Earth's radius ($d = R/2$), the acceleration due to gravity is
questions.explanation: $g' = g\left(1-\dfrac{d}{R}\right) = g\left(1-\dfrac12\right) = \dfrac{g}{2}$.

questions.q: If the Earth's radius were halved while its mass stayed the same, the escape velocity from its surface would become
questions.explanation: $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R}$, so $v_e \propto 1/\sqrt{R}$. Halving $R$ multiplies $v_e$ by $\sqrt2$.

questions.q: The escape velocity $v_e$ from a planet's surface is related to the orbital velocity $v_o$ of a satellite skimming just above the surface by
questions.explanation: $v_o = \sqrt{GM/R}$ and $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt2\,v_o$.

questions.q: Two planets orbit the Sun with orbital radii in the ratio 4 : 1. The ratio of their time periods is
questions.explanation: By Kepler's third law $T \propto r^{3/2}$, so $T_1/T_2 = (r_1/r_2)^{3/2} = 4^{3/2} = 8$.

questions.q: As a body is brought from infinity towards the Earth, its gravitational potential energy
questions.explanation: $U = -GMm/r$; as $r$ decreases, $1/r$ increases, so $U$ becomes more negative.

questions.q: Astronauts inside an orbiting space station feel weightless mainly because
options: they and the station are both in continuous free fall, accelerating toward Earth at the same rate
gravity is exactly cancelled by the vacuum of space
the station moves at constant velocity with zero acceleration
there is no gravitational force acting at that altitude
questions.explanation: Gravity at orbital altitude is still substantial; apparent weightlessness arises because the station and everything in it fall freely together, so there is no normal contact force.

questions.q: A geostationary satellite has a time period of
options: 24 hours, and it orbits in the equatorial plane
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite must match Earth's rotation period (about 24 h) and stay above a fixed point on the equator, so it must orbit in the equatorial plane.

questions.q: The escape velocity of a body from the Earth's surface
options: is inversely proportional to the mass of the body
is independent of the mass of the body being projected
increases if the body's mass increases
is directly proportional to the mass of the body
questions.explanation: $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ depends only on the mass and radius of the planet, not on the mass of the projected body.

questions.q: The universal gravitational constant $G$
options: depends on the medium between the two masses
has the same value everywhere in the universe and does not depend on the medium
increases with the masses of the interacting bodies
has different values in air and in vacuum
questions.explanation: $G$ is a fundamental constant of nature, believed to be the same everywhere and unaffected by the intervening medium.

questions.q: Using $g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$, $R = 6.4\times10^6$ m and $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$, the mass of the Earth calculated from $M = gR^2/G$ is approximately
Two satellites orbit the same planet with orbital radii in the ratio 1 : 4. The ratio of their orbital speeds is
questions.explanation: $v_o \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$, so $v_1/v_2 = \sqrt{r_2/r_1} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

questions.q: The total mechanical energy of a satellite of mass $m$ moving in a stable circular orbit of radius $r$ around a planet of mass $M$ is
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy $\frac12mv_o^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and potential energy $-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$; adding gives total energy $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, negative because the satellite is gravitationally bound.

questions.q: For a small distance $x$ from the Earth's surface ($x \ll R$), compared to the fractional decrease in $g$ on descending to depth $x$, the fractional decrease in $g$ on rising to height $x$ is
questions.explanation: For small $x$: rising gives $\Delta g/g \approx 2x/R$, while descending gives $\Delta g/g \approx x/R$ — so $g$ falls off twice as fast with height as with depth.

questions.q: Newton's law of gravitation is stated exactly for two point masses. For two uniform spherical bodies, it can still be applied by taking $r$ as
options: the distance between their nearest surfaces
questions.explanation: A uniform sphere behaves gravitationally, for points outside it, as if its entire mass were concentrated at its centre, so $r$ is measured centre to centre.

questions.q: Kepler's second law (a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals) is a direct consequence of the conservation of
questions.explanation: Gravitational force on a planet is central (along the line to the Sun), so it exerts no torque about the Sun; hence angular momentum, and therefore areal velocity, stays constant.

questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity on the Earth's surface is slightly less at the equator than at the poles. This is mainly due to
options: Earth's rotation and its equatorial bulge, both of which reduce effective g at the equator
the Moon being closer to the equator
atmospheric pressure being higher at the equator
the Sun's gravitational pull being stronger at the equator
questions.explanation: Earth's rotation produces an outward effect greatest at the equator, and the equatorial radius is also larger due to the bulge (g \propto 1/R^2); both effects lower g there compared to the poles.

questions.q: Treating the Earth as a uniform solid sphere, the acceleration due to gravity at its centre is
options: equal to the surface value g
questions.explanation: $g' = g(1-d/R)$; at the centre $d=R$, so $g'=0$. Only the mass enclosed within radius $r$ contributes, and none is enclosed at $r=0$.

questions.q: A planet $P_1$ orbits the Sun with a time period of 1 year at distance $r$. Another planet $P_2$ orbits at distance $4r$. Using Kepler's third law, the time period of $P_2$ is
questions.explanation: $T \propto r^{3/2}$, so $T_2 = T_1(4)^{3/2} = 1\times8 = 8$ years.

questions.q: A satellite orbiting just above Earth's surface (radius $R$) has time period $T_0$. Another satellite orbits at height $h=R$ above the surface (orbital radius $2R$). Its time period is
The minimum energy that must be supplied to a satellite of mass $m$, moving in a circular orbit of radius $r$ about a planet of mass $M$, to send it to infinity (its binding energy) is
questions.explanation: Total energy of the orbit is $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$. To take the satellite to infinity (zero energy), an energy $+\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ must be supplied — this is the binding energy.

questions.q: The Moon has about 1/4 the Earth's radius and about 1/6 its surface gravity. If Earth's escape velocity is 11.2 km/s, the Moon's escape velocity is closest to
questions.explanation: $v_e=\sqrt{2gR}$, so $v_{e,\text{moon}}/v_{e,\text{earth}} = \sqrt{(1/6)(1/4)} = \sqrt{1/24}\approx0.204$; $0.204\times11.2\approx2.3$ km/s.

questions.q: Two planets have equal acceleration due to gravity at their surfaces, but planet B has twice the radius of planet A. The ratio of their mean densities $\rho_A:\rho_B$ is
questions.explanation: $g=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$, so for equal $g$, $\rho R$ is constant; with $R_B=2R_A$, $\rho_B=\rho_A/2$, giving $\rho_A:\rho_B=2:1$.

questions.q: Two point masses $m$ and $4m$ are separated by a distance $d$. The gravitational potential at the midpoint of the line joining them is
questions.explanation: Each mass is $d/2$ from the midpoint: $V=-\dfrac{Gm}{d/2}-\dfrac{G(4m)}{d/2} = -\dfrac{2Gm}{d}-\dfrac{8Gm}{d} = -\dfrac{10Gm}{d}$.

questions.q: Point masses $m$ and $4m$ are fixed a distance $d$ apart. The point on the line joining them where the resultant gravitational field is zero lies at a distance from $m$ equal to
questions.explanation: Setting $\dfrac{Gm}{x^2}=\dfrac{G(4m)}{(d-x)^2}$ gives $d-x=2x$, so $x=d/3$.

questions.q: For an artificial satellite moving in a stable circular orbit, its kinetic energy $K$ and potential energy $U$ are related by
questions.explanation: $K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=-2K$.

questions.q: If the Earth suddenly stopped rotating about its axis (its shape unchanged), the apparent weight of a body resting at the equator would
questions.explanation: Currently part of the true gravitational force at the equator supplies the centripetal force for rotation, reducing apparent weight; if rotation stops, this requirement vanishes and the full gravitational force is felt as weight, so apparent weight increases.

questions.q: Two identical satellites A and B orbit the same planet in circular orbits of radii $r$ and $4r$ respectively. The ratio of their kinetic energies $K_A:K_B$ is
questions.explanation: $K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\propto\dfrac1r$, so $K_A:K_B = \dfrac{1/r}{1/4r} = 4:1$.

questions.q: The energy required to shift a satellite of mass $m$ from a circular orbit of radius $r$ to one of radius $2r$, around a planet of mass $M$, is
questions.explanation: $E_1=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, $E_2=-\dfrac{GMm}{4r}$; energy needed $=E_2-E_1=\dfrac{GMm}{4r}$.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A planet moves fastest when closest to the Sun (perihelion) and slowest when farthest (aphelion). Reason (R): The planet's angular momentum about the Sun is conserved, so a smaller orbital radius must be compensated by a larger speed to keep the areal velocity constant.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is a correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Kepler's second law follows from conservation of angular momentum; as $r$ decreases near the Sun, $v$ must increase to keep angular momentum (and areal velocity) constant, making the planet fastest at perihelion.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about gravitation is INCORRECT?
options: The acceleration due to gravity of a freely falling body is independent of its mass.
Escape velocity from a planet's surface does not depend on the angle at which the body is projected.
The gravitational constant $G$ has the same value in air, water and vacuum.
The gravitational force between two point masses depends on the medium separating them.
questions.explanation: Unlike electrostatic force, which can be modified by a dielectric medium, gravitational force is unaffected by the intervening medium — statement D is false.

questions.q: The orbital speed of a satellite moving in a circular orbit around a planet depends on
options: the mass of the planet and the orbital radius, but not on the satellite's mass
the mass of the satellite only
the mass of the satellite and the orbital radius
the mass of the planet only, irrespective of orbital radius
questions.explanation: $v_o=\sqrt{GM/r}$ depends on the planet's mass $M$ and orbital radius $r$; the satellite's own mass cancels out.

questions.q: If the mass of the Earth were 4 times its present value while its radius stayed the same, the escape velocity from its surface would become
questions.explanation: $v_e=\sqrt{2GM/R}\propto\sqrt M$; quadrupling $M$ multiplies $v_e$ by $\sqrt4=2$.

questions.q: A hypothetical planet has the same mass as Earth but half its radius. Taking Earth's escape velocity as 11.2 km/s, the escape velocity from this planet is approximately
questions.explanation: $v_e\propto1/\sqrt R$ for the same $M$; halving $R$ multiplies $v_e$ by $\sqrt2$: $11.2\times\sqrt2\approx15.8$ km/s.

questions.q: A graph of the acceleration due to gravity $g$ against distance $r$ from Earth's centre rises linearly from zero at $r=0$ to a maximum at the surface ($r=R$), then falls off following an inverse-square curve for $r>R$. This shape arises because
options: gravity does not exist inside solid matter
g is constant everywhere inside and outside the Earth
inside the Earth only the mass enclosed within radius $r$ pulls the point (growing with $r$), while outside the entire mass acts as if concentrated at the centre, giving $1/r^2$ fall-off
the density of the Earth is exactly uniform outside the surface as well
questions.explanation: Inside, $g\propto r$ because enclosed mass $\propto r^3$ so $g=GM_{enc}/r^2 \propto r$; outside, all mass $M$ acts from the centre giving the standard $1/r^2$ decrease.

questions.q: Gravitational potential energy of a two-mass system is conventionally taken to be zero when the separation between the masses is
options: equal to the sum of their radii
questions.explanation: By convention, $U=-GMm/r \to 0$ as $r\to\infty$, which is chosen as the reference (zero) level of gravitational potential energy.

questions.q: Newton's law of gravitation obeys Newton's third law, meaning that
options: only the more massive body exerts a force
gravitational forces do not occur in pairs
the smaller body feels a smaller-magnitude force than the larger body exerts
the two mutual gravitational forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, acting on the two different bodies
questions.explanation: By Newton's third law, the force each mass exerts on the other is equal in magnitude ($Gm_1m_2/r^2$ for both) and opposite in direction, even though the masses differ.
